study.title: Acts 8 - persecution, expansion of the gospel, and the inclusion of new peoples
study.overview: Acts 8 shows how the persecution that came upon the church in Jerusalem did not interrupt the work of God; on the contrary, he scattered the believers and brought the word of Christ to new places. Philip preaches in Samaria, where the gospel is accompanied by signs, joy, and confrontation with the magic of Simon. Then the apostles confirm the work among the Samaritans with prayer and laying on of hands, showing the unity of the church and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Finally, Philip is led by God to the way of Gaza, where he announces Jesus to an Ethiopian officer who reads Isaiah, is baptized and follows his way with joy. The chapter ends with Philip continuing to preach in cities until he reaches Caesarea.

outline.title: Persecution in Jerusalem and missionary dispersion
outline.explanation: After Stephen's death, the persecution intensifies. Saul consents to his death and acts against the church, but the scattered do not silence: they continue to announce the word where they go. The suffering, instead of shutting the gospel, spreads it.

outline.title: Philip in Samaria and the falsehood of Simon
outline.explanation: Philip preaches Christ in Samaria, accompanied by signs and healings, and the city experiences great joy. Many believe and are baptized, including Simon, though their admiration for the signs reveals a still confused faith. The passage prepares the contrast between God's work and the attempt to use spiritual power for human purposes.

outline.title: The Apostles, the Holy Spirit, and the Rebuke Simon
outline.explanation: The apostles send Peter and John to confirm the new Samaritan believers. The reception of the Holy Spirit shows that the work in Samaria is authentic and not inferior to that of Jerusalem. Simon tries to buy the power of God, but Peter confronts him firmly, calling him to repentance and forgiveness.

outline.title: The Ethiopian, Isaiah, and the advancement of the gospel
outline.explanation: Guided by an angel and the Spirit, Philip finds an Ethiopian who read Isaiah without understanding the text. Philip announces Jesus from that Scripture, and man believes, asks for baptism and follows joyful. The chapter closes with the continuation of Philip's mission in several cities to Caesarea.

study.context: The chapter takes place after Stephen's death, when a great persecution of the church appears in Jerusalem. The notes inform that believers were scattered by Judea and Samaria, and that this paved the way for the spread of the gospel. Samaria appears as a place where there was a strong tension of acceptance between Jews and Samaritans, and the sending of Peter and John there is described as an impressive step to overcome prejudices. There is also the scene of the Ethiopian officer, an eunuch attached to the queen of the Ethiopians, who returns from Jerusalem by reading the prophet Isaiah. The notes indicate that he traveled from Jerusalem to worship and that Philip then continues to preach to Nitrogen and Caesarea.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God rules to persecution to extend the scope of his word. The gospel is not bound to Jerusalem: he reaches Samaria and then an African foreigner, showing that God's promise extends beyond ethnic and religious boundaries. The signs in Samaria confirm the message, but do not replace the gospel; the center remains Christ. The laying on of hands and the prayer of the apostles highlight the unity of the church and the reality of the Holy Spirit as a gift of God, not as a human technique. The rebuke to Simon shows that the gifts of God cannot be bought or manipulated; the heart must be upright before God, and repentance is the way to forgiveness. In the Ethiopian episode, Scripture is interpreted Christologically: Isaiah points to Jesus, whose humiliation and suffering are the basis of good news.

scholarViews.insight: Persecution did not weaken the church; the scattered believers simply brought the good news about Jesus to where they were.
The gospel came to Samaria and was received there, showing that God's work prospers even when the church suffers.
The Ethiopian eunuch had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and upon returning, he used the time in the reading of Isaiah, which shows his religious seriousness and his need for instruction.

questions: How do we react when the pressure, loss or opposition scatters us: in silence, or continuing to witness to Christ?
Is there in us the temptation to treat spiritual gifts as something to be controlled, displayed or bought, as Simon tried to do?
Do we read Scripture with the desire to be taught by God, as the Ethiopian, or just to fulfill a religious routine?
study.practice: This week, choose a situation of dispersion, interruption or unexpected change and decide to turn it into a witness opportunity. Pray before talking to someone, read a Bible passage carefully and explain with simplicity who Jesus is and what he did. Also examine your heart: ask God to reveal any desire to use faith for personal gain, prestige or control, and practice concrete repentance, with confession and change of attitude.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow to safely affirm additional historical details beyond the mentioned ones, such as exact dates, archaeological context or broader identification of nitrogen and Caesarea beyond what was cited. It is also not possible to accurately define Simão's internal state beyond what the text and commentators suggest; their faith should be read with caution. The understanding of the exact way of the relationship between the events in Samaria and the reception of the Holy Spirit depends on the biblical account itself and the interpretations of the notes, which may differ.
